content: 1. Pharmacological methods for pain control during medical abortion include the use of ibuprofen, acetaminophen combined with codeine, antiemetics, loperamide, and tramadol. These medications can be administered either prophylactically (before the onset of pain) or after pain has begun. Intravenous opiates and paracervical blocks (PCB) are also options for pain management. 2. Non-pharmacological methods for pain control include interventions such as music therapy, acupuncture, and the use of techniques like verbicaine. These approaches aim to provide relief without the use of medications. 3. In some cases, no treatment or the use of a placebo may be considered. The effectiveness of pain control methods is typically measured by the maximum pain level reported on a Visual Analog Scale (VAS). Safety is assessed by monitoring complications related to pain control methods, the use of supplemental narcotics, additional analgesic medications, and any associated side effects. 4. The effectiveness of medical abortion regimens is defined by successful completion without the need for additional surgical intervention. Other outcomes include the time to expulsion, patient satisfaction, and acceptability of the method. 5. For pregnant individuals seeking medical abortion at 14 weeks of gestation or later, the question arises whether pain control using specific pharmacological or non-pharmacological methods is safer, more effective, or more satisfactory compared to other methods or no treatment at all. 6. Cervical priming before surgical abortion is evaluated for its effectiveness, safety, and acceptability. For pregnancies under 12 weeks, cervical priming can be achieved using medications or mechanical methods. Comparisons are made with placebo or different regimens of medications and mechanical techniques. 7. For pregnancies at or beyond 12 weeks, cervical priming with mifepristone plus misoprostol, mifepristone alone, or misoprostol alone is assessed for safety, effectiveness, and acceptability. Outcomes include pre-procedure cervical dilation, the need for further dilation, ease of the procedure, and time to complete the procedure. 8. Cervical priming with medications plus laminaria is compared to laminaria alone for surgical abortion at or beyond 12 weeks. The effectiveness, safety, and acceptability of these methods are evaluated. 9. Mechanical methods of cervical priming, such as laminaria, Foley bulbs, or Dilapan, are compared to other mechanical methods for their safety, effectiveness, and acceptability in preparation for dilation and evacuation (D&E) procedures at or beyond 12 weeks of gestation. 10. Medical abortion using letrozole plus misoprostol is compared to misoprostol alone for its safety, effectiveness, and acceptability. Outcomes include ongoing pregnancy rates, completion without surgical intervention, expulsion time, patient satisfaction, and cost. 11. Medical abortion with letrozole plus misoprostol is also compared to mifepristone plus misoprostol for similar outcomes, including safety, effectiveness, and patient satisfaction. 12. The combination of mifepristone and letrozole is evaluated against misoprostol alone for medical abortion. Outcomes include ongoing pregnancy rates, completion without surgical intervention, expulsion time, safety, and cost. 13. For missed abortion at less than 14 weeks of gestation, medical management with mifepristone plus misoprostol is compared to misoprostol alone. Effectiveness is measured by the rate of failed expulsion or retained products, completion without surgical intervention, and safety outcomes. 14. Medical management of missed abortion using all available regimens is compared to expectant management. Outcomes include effectiveness, safety, expulsion time, patient satisfaction, and cost. 15. Surgical management of missed abortion is evaluated as an alternative to medical or expectant management for its safety, effectiveness, and acceptability. 16. Self-management of medical abortion, including self-assessment of eligibility, administration of medications, and evaluation of outcomes, is assessed for its safety, effectiveness, and acceptability compared to management by trained health workers. Outcomes include success rates, safety, physical and emotional experiences, and cost. 17. Self-assessment of eligibility for medical abortion is compared to eligibility assessment by trained health workers. Outcomes include the accuracy of assessments, ongoing pregnancy rates, completion without surgical intervention, safety, and patient satisfaction. 18. Self-administration of medications for medical abortion, with instructions from a reliable source, is compared to administration by trained health workers. Outcomes include adherence to the regimen, effectiveness, safety, and patient satisfaction. 19. Self-assessment of the outcome of medical abortion is evaluated as an alternative to assessment by trained health workers. Outcomes include the success of the abortion, safety, and patient satisfaction. 20. Pharmacy workers providing accurate information about abortion care, including the availability of safe providers, is assessed for its safety, effectiveness, and acceptability.
